I ran your melting-magnet experiment as one job with 4 circuits and 250 shots each. The job ran on IQM's free Emerald test device, emerald:mock. The job ID is 01a16489-3a64-7189-a38a-05d16b804bc6, and it completed. Test-device jobs cost 0 credits.

What I built: each circuit uses all 54 qubits of Emerald, one qubit per atom, and every qubit starts in 0. The real Emerald currently lists 83 CZ couplers. The test device lists 90, so I used only the 83 that the real chip lists. One QB50 has no working coupler on the real chip right now, so it feels only the sideways field. One time step is a sideways-field turn RX(theta) on every qubit, then exp(i pi/4 ZZ) on every coupler. Each coupler interaction is exactly one CZ gate plus turns about the Z axis. I folded those Z turns into the phases of the later field pulses, so they add no gates. I wrote the circuits directly in IQM's native gate format and skipped the compiler, so nothing could add, merge, or remove a gate. This matters most at theta = 0, where a compiler would cancel pairs of CZ gates across steps. I read the circuits back from the server. Each one has 249 CZ gates, which is 83 couplers times 3 steps, and each coupler appears exactly 3 times. Each circuit measures QB1 to QB54.

Magnetization is the average of Z over the 54 qubits. Z is +1 for bit 0 and -1 for bit 1.

theta = 0: a perfect machine gives 1.000. The test device gave -0.011.
theta = 0.2 pi: a perfect machine gives 0.446. The test device gave 0.009.
theta = 0.35 pi: a perfect machine gives 0.102. The test device gave -0.033.
theta = 0.5 pi: a perfect machine gives 0.000. The test device gave 0.040.

I computed the perfect-machine numbers exactly from the circuits I submitted, without any noise. The last coupler layer does not change any Z value. Because of that, each qubit's Z value depends only on qubits at most 2 couplers away. I simulated that small neighborhood around each qubit with a full quantum simulation. I also checked that a 3-coupler neighborhood gives the same numbers, and that my native gates match the textbook circuit.

What the perfect machine shows: with no sideways field, every spin stays up, so the magnetization stays at 1. As the field gets stronger, it tips the spins over, and the coupler interactions mix up their directions. The magnetization falls to 0.45 at 0.2 pi and to 0.10 at 0.35 pi. At 0.5 pi it reaches exactly 0, so the sheet's magnetization has fully melted. The principle is that a sideways (transverse) field fights the up-down order, and the spin-spin interactions spread that disorder across the sheet.

What the test device shows: all 4 measured values are close to 0 and do not follow the field. This is expected. The emerald:mock device checks that the circuits are valid and returns made-up bitstrings that do not come from running the circuit. Its numbers tell you nothing about the physics. To see the real melting curve, the same job would need to run on the real Emerald. That costs credits at about 0.75 credits per second, and I did not run it.

The counts field holds the last circuit's counts (theta = 0.5 pi). counts_list holds all 4 circuits in order. The job ID is in job_log.txt in the worktree. The scripts are /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_8d7e6233-d69-24/work/build.py and /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_8d7e6233-d69-24/work/analyze.py.
